assessments.title: Internal Energy, Heat, and Work
assessments.objectives: Distinguish stored internal energy from heat and work transfers; explain expansion/compression; calculate constant-pressure boundary work and interpret energy arrows.
assessments.difficulty: Beginner through application; final question is a challenge
assessments.instructions: Use ΔU=Q−W: Q positive into the system and W positive by the system. Show the equation, signed substitution, arithmetic and units for numerical answers. Explain physical meaning. Use given constants. Retain intermediate digits and round final answers as requested; for unspecified precision, accept sensible rounding. Graphs and data are simulated educational models.

questions.prompt: Classify U, Q and W as a stored state property or a transfer during a process. Explain why the phrase “stored work” is misleading.
A gas is compressed by an external piston. Is work BY the gas positive or negative in this unit? What sign describes work ON it?
Which can occur in a rigid closed container? A. Pressure-volume boundary work from a moving wall. B. Energy input by an electrical interaction across the system boundary. Explain.
choices: B. Electrical energy input across the boundary

questions.prompt: Convert a 450 mL volume increase into liters. State the energy unit equivalent to kPa·L.
A gas expands from 1.5 L to 4.0 L against constant external pressure 80 kPa. Calculate signed work by the gas.
A gas is compressed from .0060 m³ to .0020 m³ against constant 125000 Pa. Calculate work BY the gas and the magnitude of work supplied ON it.
Use the WS 21 piston diagram. Label the work arrow during expansion and compression as entering or leaving the gas. Explain why these arrows are not heat arrows.

Challenge: An ideal gas freely expands into vacuum inside an insulated rigid enclosure. Its occupied volume increases. Is W=P_extΔV positive? Determine W and Q, and explain why the volume change alone is insufficient.

reference_material.description: Schematic expansion/compression against a load. Arrows indicate piston motion; identify the corresponding mechanical energy-transfer direction for the gas. Not a scale drawing.
reference_material.figure_alt: Gas pushes piston outward in expansion; surroundings push inward in compression.

questions.prompt: State the Unit 4 first law and define both transfer signs.
A gas receives 90 J of heat and does 30 J of work. Find ΔU.
A source says 40 J of work is done ON the gas. What value belongs in W in ΔU=Q−W?
True or false: If ΔU=0, both Q and W must be zero. Give a numerical counterexample or justification.
A closed gas releases 120 J as heat while surroundings do 200 J of work on it. Calculate ΔU and explain the direction of its change.
A process has ΔU=−150 J and W=+250 J. Find Q and explain how heat input can accompany decreasing U.
Use the WS 22 energy ledger: 600 J heat enters, 100 J heat leaves and 220 J work leaves the gas. Calculate net Q and ΔU.
Challenge: Routes A and B connect exactly the same initial and final states of a closed gas. A has Q=400 J and W=150 J. B has W=−50 J. Find ΔU for each and Q for B; explain why the heats can differ.

reference_material.description: All arrows cross the boundary of one closed gas system. Whole-system motion and height changes are negligible. The heat arrows are separate transfers, not already net quantities.
reference_material.figure_alt: 600 J heat enters,100 J heat leaves,220 J work leaves.

questions.prompt: Define isothermal. Does merely ending at the starting temperature prove that an entire process was isothermal?
A fixed ideal gas doubles its volume isothermally. What happens to its absolute pressure?
For fixed ideal gas undergoing isothermal expansion, choose the correct statement: A. Q=0 always. B. ΔU=0 and Q=W. Explain.
Why should an isothermal melting process not automatically be assigned ΔU=0 using the ideal-gas rule?
Fixed ideal gas starts at 300 kPa and 2.0 L. It expands isothermally to 5.0 L. Find final absolute pressure.
A fixed ideal gas does 180 J of work during isothermal expansion. Find Q and ΔU.
Use the WS 23 curve. Verify PV at A and B, then state why P_A(V_B−V_A) is not a valid work calculation for this curved path.

Challenge: Surroundings do 110 J of work ON a fixed ideal gas compressed isothermally. A student writes Q=+110 J because “compression heats gas.” Correct the signs and explain how temperature remains fixed.

reference_material.description: Fixed amount of ideal gas on a slow, mechanically balanced isothermal expansion. The curve has PV=600 kPa·L. Do not calculate its curved-path work using a rectangle.
reference_material.figure_alt: A at2 L and300 kPa; B at5 L and120 kPa.

questions.prompt: Define adiabatic. Which quantity is constrained to zero?
Adiabatic gas does 70 J of work. Calculate ΔU.
Explain why rapid motion alone does not prove a process is exactly adiabatic.
An insulated gas is compressed and 90 J of work is done on it. Give W_by and ΔU.
Adiabatic ideal gas begins at 310 K with supplied C_U=10 J/K. It does 150 J of work. Find final temperature.
Use the qualitative WS 24 graph. At the same enlarged volume, which path has lower pressure: reversible adiabatic or isothermal expansion from the same initial ideal-gas state? Explain.
An insulated ideal gas expands into vacuum with no resisting load. Compare its endpoint ΔU and ΔT with those of an adiabatic expansion that does positive work.
Challenge: A gas with C_U=8 J/K falls from 300 K to 280 K while doing 200 J of work. Is the process adiabatic? Calculate Q and justify.

reference_material.description: Conceptual comparison only: reversible ideal-gas expansion from the same state. Arbitrary-unit axes have no quantitative ticks. Use the relative curves, not invented numerical coordinates.
reference_material.figure_alt: Adiabatic expansion falls below the isotherm at the same enlarged volume.

questions.prompt: Match isochoric and isobaric with (a) constant volume, (b) constant pressure. State which is a vertical line on a standard P–V graph.
A fixed ideal gas at constant volume warms from 300 K to 330 K. If initial pressure is 100 kPa, find final pressure.
A rigid gas container receives 60 J of heat; no other work occurs. Find pressure-volume work and ΔU.
Why can a constant-pressure warming ideal gas require more heat than its increase in internal energy?
Fixed ideal gas at constant pressure has V_i=3.0 L at 27.0 °C. It warms to 87.0 °C. Find V_f using 273.15 for the Celsius-to-Kelvin offset.
Balanced isobaric expansion at 120 kPa takes gas from 2.0 to 4.5 L. If ΔU=180 J and only PV work occurs, find W and Q.
Use the WS 25 paths. For A→B→D, calculate work on the vertical stage and horizontal stage. Compare total work with A→C→D.
Challenge: A student says “the gas is insulated, so pressure is constant and no work occurs.” Identify each error and state what insulation actually permits you to conclude.

reference_material.description: Fixed gas, mechanically balanced paths, only PV work. A→B→D and A→C→D are two alternatives, not one closed cycle. Straight horizontal/vertical segments are exact model assumptions.
reference_material.figure_alt: Upper route expands at200 kPa; lower route at100 kPa.

questions.prompt: What must return to its starting value in a complete thermodynamic cycle: U, total heat transferred, or total work transferred? Explain.
On a P-vertical, V-horizontal diagram, what sign is net PV work by the gas for a simple clockwise loop?
A cycle receives net 300 J of heat. Determine ΔU_cycle and W_net.
A gas moves vertically on a standard P–V plot. What is its PV work and why?
Use the WS 26 rectangle A→B→C→D→A. Find the work on each horizontal segment and the net work.
A clockwise triangular cycle encloses a right triangle with base 3.0 L and pressure height 160 kPa. Find net work and net heat per cycle.
A cycle absorbs 900 J and rejects 650 J. Find W_net. If it completes 4 cycles each second at these values, find average mechanical output power.
Challenge: Reverse the WS 26 rectangular cycle. Find signed W_net and Q_net. Explain why negative work by the gas means work input, and why the diagram alone does not fully specify a refrigerator.

reference_material.description: Clockwise cycle A→B→C→D→A. Mechanically balanced, only PV work, closed gas returns to its original state. All segments are horizontal or vertical.
reference_material.figure_alt: Rectangle from1 to5 L and80 to200 kPa with clockwise arrows.

questions.prompt: In an engine balance, Q_H and Q_C are defined as positive heat magnitudes. Write the cycle work equation and efficiency equation.
An engine produces 240 J of work from 800 J heat input. Calculate efficiency as a fraction and a percent.
Why does the efficiency denominator use heat absorbed rather than net heat for a complete cycle?
Convert 76.85 °C and 26.85 °C to Kelvin for a reservoir-ratio calculation.
An engine absorbs 1500 J per cycle and rejects 1050 J. Find work and thermal efficiency.
An engine supplies 360 J/cycle at efficiency.40. Determine required Q_H and Q_C.
Reservoirs are at 500 K and 300 K. Find the maximum ideal efficiency and decide whether a claimed 45% engine between them is possible.
Challenge: Use the WS 27 reservoir diagram: hot 126.85 °C, cold 26.85 °C; Q_H=1200 J/cycle. Find maximum work output and minimum rejected heat. Explain why real work is lower.

reference_material.description: Two-reservoir cyclic heat-engine model. Input is a positive heat magnitude of1200 J/cycle. Temperatures are given in Celsius and require conversion for the ideal bound.

questions.prompt: State the natural direction of net heat transfer between two objects with different temperatures and no external driving device.
Does a refrigerator moving heat from cold food to a warmer room violate the second law? Explain.

Which is a more reliable entropy statement? A. Entropy is simply visible messiness. B. Entropy is a state property related to microscopic energy distribution, and total entropy of an isolated combination cannot decrease. Explain.
choices: B. Entropy is a state property with an isolated-total constraint

questions.prompt: State the unit of entropy and explain why it should not be confused with internal energy.
Supplied entropy changes for a complete isolated combination are ΔS_system=−3 J/K and ΔS_surroundings=+5 J/K. Find the total and assess consistency with the second law.
A claimed isolated process has supplied changes +1 J/K for the system and−2 J/K for all its surroundings. Find total entropy change and assess the claim.
A working gas completes a cycle and returns to its initial entropy. Does this prove the cycle is reversible? Explain with the surroundings included.

Challenge: A proposed cyclic engine takes 1000 J from 600 K, rejects 300 J to 300 K, and delivers 700 J work. Check both energy conservation and the two-reservoir efficiency limit. Which law rules it out?
